claims.text: A data-driven machine-learning framework can rapidly screen the high-dimensional composition space of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Machine-learning screening will identify RHEAs with a better combination of intrinsic strength, ductility, and density than traditional iterative thermo-kinetic methods.
Conventional RHEA formulations are developed through slow, iterative thermo-kinetic analysis and simulation.
The proposed model would be trained on high-throughput experimental and simulation data.
The training data would correlate elemental attributes such as density, melting point, and phase-stability indicators with mechanical properties.
The screening is intended for multicomponent refractory alloys under conditions relevant to high-temperature, high-performance applications.
Alloy composition controls local lattice distortions and phase stability.
Local lattice distortions and phase stability mediate mechanical behavior.
The machine-learning model can exploit correlations among elemental properties, processing parameters, and alloy performance.
The model can predict compositions that simultaneously reduce density and provide high intrinsic strength and ductility.
Machine-learning prediction can bypass a time-consuming iterative alloy-design cycle.
The method will rapidly identify RHEAs with improved tensile properties and lower weight than conventionally designed baseline alloys.
Established thermo-kinetic and simulation approaches have longer iterative cycles and yield less optimal property combinations.
The machine-learning approach is expected to be effective where sufficient high-throughput training data are available.
Predictions may be less reliable in sparsely sampled or extreme composition regions.
The magnitude and generalizability of property improvements depend on the quality and representativeness of the training data.
Machine-learning-predicted and conventionally designed alloys can be compared using matched processing histories, tensile tests, and density measurements.
The hypothesis is falsified if predicted alloys fail to show statistically significant simultaneous improvements in tensile strength, elongation, and density relative to controls.
